b. Taenarian: Pherecydes in the ninth book (3 fg 39 J.) says: "that Elatus son of Icarius marries Erimede daughter of Damasiclus; and of them is born Taenarus, from whom the city and the cape and the harbor are called Taenarum." LmP
21 Stephanus of Byzantium, Ταίναρος: ... there is also Taenarus the son of Icarius (Meineke adds "son of Elatus"), from whom the city and the cape and the harbor are named. cf. W 93
22 Ἔλατος (in P) : Λύλατος in L : Ἀλήτης in Apollodorus, Bibliotheca III 126 | Ἰκαρίου Meineke : Ἰκάρου | Δαμασίππου in Apollodorus, Bibliotheca l. l.

c. κεινὴν ὁδόν: meaning "vain." The sense: for both of these, if they had joined the voyage, would have relieved the Argonauts of all their toils. Apollonius here gives the reason why they did not sail with them. It is also read κείνην with barytone accent as an anaphoric reference, and κεινὴν with oxytone accent meaning κενήν ("empty").
2 πάντας Fr. : -ων | 4 after αὐτούς A adds δεσμοῖς γάρ, φησί, κατείχοντο ἐν τῷ Ἅιδῃ διὰ τὸ βουληθῆναι ἁρπάσαι τὴν Περσεφόνην. cf. W 29

105-08a. Tiphys son of Hagnias: Siphae is a city of Boeotia, and Siphaean is a deme of the Thespians; Thespeia is also a city of Thessaly. Pherecydes (3 fg 107 J.) records that Tiphys was the son of Ponteus, but Aeschylus in his Argo (fg 21 N.2) calls Tiphys "Iphys."

b. προδαῆναι: to learn beforehand. For this is the skill of a good helmsman. The meaning: he was good at judging the time for sailing by the sun by day, and by night by reference to some of the stars.
109. Tritonis: There are three Tritons: of Boeotia, of Thessaly, of Libya; and in the one in Libya Athena was born.
112. 〈κείνης ὑποθημοσύνῃσι:〉 because it came about through the counsels of Athena. Lg

115. Phleias, and after him: A city of the Peloponnese, Araethyrea, now called Phlius, from Phlius, son of Dionysus and Chthonophyle. Phlius lies on the borders of Sicyon. And Dionysus himself was called Phlius, from φλεῖν ("to abound") in wine, that is, to flourish.

17 Stephanus of Byzantium, Φλιοῦς: a city of the Peloponnese, formerly Araethyrea and Aranteia, from Phlius, son of Dionysus and Chthonophyle. ... It is named from φλεῖν, which means "to be fruitful." cf. W 93 | Strabo VIII 382 | sch. D B 571 | 20 Socrates of Cos, fg 4 Tresp (Φλεύς)
